comments.author: @ChaseFreedomMusician
comments.text:
I appreciate the follow-up video and the concept of the "Jagged Frontier." It’s a great way to illustrate how these models can excel in certain areas, like math, physics, or chemistry, while struggling with tasks that seem simple to humans, such as counting letters in a word or solving trick questions. But I want to emphasize that those kinds of gaps—the things these systems can’t do yet—aren’t part of my argument. I’m not concerned about whether they can solve the strawberry problem or handle “gotcha” questions. My point is about the system itself, not its current limitations. Those gaps don’t define whether or not it’s AGI.

To clarify, I’ve never said these models aren’t intelligent. They’re incredibly intelligent and represent a monumental achievement in AI. I also believe they’re AGI-adjacent in some ways—pushing the boundaries of computation and reasoning, and perhaps even laying the groundwork for creating AGI in the future. But the "G" in AGI—general—is what separates it from what we have now. AGI isn’t just about excelling at certain tasks or reasoning through complex problems with test-time computation. It’s about the ability to generalize, adapt, and learn dynamically across an unlimited range of tasks without retraining or manual intervention. That’s the line we haven’t crossed yet.

A lot of the discussion seems to focus on prompts and context windows as ways to enable these systems to "learn." But prompts are inherently limited. They can only hold a finite amount of information, and the model doesn’t retain or integrate what it learns in a way that updates its core understanding. This is where the distinction becomes clear: AGI wouldn’t just process a task within the confines of a context window—it would take insights from solving one problem and apply them broadly to others. It wouldn’t need to repeat the same compute-intensive reasoning process every time because it would have already evolved its understanding. And to this point, there’s often confusion between caching and generalization. If a system becomes faster at answering the same question the second time, that’s not generalization—it’s caching. True generalization means understanding the core principles of a problem and applying those principles to entirely new situations.

This is why I don’t consider models like 03 to be AGI. They’re brilliant expert systems—highly intelligent and transformative in their capabilities. They’re solving monumental problems and paving the way for even greater advancements. Take the Riemann Hypothesis and satisfiability problems, for example. These are two of the most profound challenges in mathematics and computer science, and models like 03 could help us tackle them in ways we’ve never been able to before. Solving the Riemann Hypothesis could reshape our understanding of prime numbers, leading to breakthroughs in cryptography and computational efficiency. And advancing SAT problem-solving could revolutionize fields like logistics, healthcare, and AI optimization itself.

These achievements are extraordinary. They have the potential to solve problems that humanity has struggled with for centuries, and they might even help us create AGI someday. But solving specific problems—even incredibly important ones—doesn’t make a system AGI. AGI is about adaptability, generalization, and the ability to learn and grow autonomously. It’s not just a collection of tools or reasoning processes—it’s a fundamentally different kind of intelligence.

So, let me be clear: I think what’s happening here is amazing. Models like 03 are a testament to how far we’ve come, and they’re going to change the world in significant ways. But they’re still operating as highly advanced, specialized systems. They’re intelligent, yes. They’re transformative, absolutely. But they’re not AGI. That’s not a criticism—it’s just about being precise with our definitions.

comments.author: @moxes8237
comments.text:
When someone speaks of general intelligence as we have it, they are not referring to the specific things we know or have studied. They are referring to our ability to learn “generally.” For example, if I were taught to paint at a young age and continued to learn and practice until adulthood, I would likely become very skilled at painting.

The argument many people make about why large language models have reached AGI often goes something like this: “I don’t know what a doctor knows, but the fact that ChatGPT can perform tasks at that level proves it has general intelligence because it can do something I, as a human with general intelligence, cannot.” However, what I am trying to convey is that it’s not that I am unable to do it, it’s that I’ve never paid attention to being a doctor, so I know nothing about it. If I had been raised and trained to be a doctor from a young age, I could become one as an adult without needing any additional “hardware” to learn it. My brain would be the same when acquiring the ability to paint as it would be when studying to become a doctor.

Current AI models are not general because they lack this capability. They cannot, for instance, both draw and write a joke using the same model. Instead, they require specialized models like Sora for videos, DALL-E for images, and ChatGPT for text. This is known as narrow artificial intelligence. Currently, we are stitching together models, creating the illusion of generality. In reality, we are combining a model that plays the game of Go with a model that plays chess and calling it general.

Models are also split in the way they learn. For example, some models learn through data alone, while others learn through reinforcement learning, doing something over and over until they eventually get it. We, as humans, can learn in all the ways different models learn using a single “model”, our brain.

To drive the message home, current models, for lack of a better word, “learn” in 2D, while we learn in 3D. If you were to take a picture of both outputs, they might look the same because a picture is two-dimensional. This is where I think many people misunderstand what general intelligence is, they are looking at a 2D picture of a 3D world.

comments.text:
I'm pretty positive that any submission attempting to solve the ARC-AGI problems is allowed to have an algorithm that translates the two-dimensional matrix input into a two-dimensional visual input, and I think they even supply the contestants with such a software. A two-dimensional matrix input is, if anything, making things easier on "matrix-abstraction AIs" so that they don't need to also have image recognition.

One big point where I agree with Mr. Chollet is that it's important to distinguish between widely useful  or superintelligent AI on one hand, and general AI on the other. General AI would be AI that can learn a wide variety of new skills, not just one that already excels at a particular range of skills by default.

Just looking at your three examples for extremely impressive AI, for example - curing cancer, solving the Riemann Hypothesis, and organizing the world's energy supply - all three of those are extremely large-scale, slow, pretty theoretical problems where giving one correct output per year would be impressive enough to change the entire world.
As impressive as that would be, that is actually a pretty narrow set of problems - very different for example from walking a bipedal robot, or deciding what to cook and cooking it, or writing lines of text with a consistent rhythm or word count, or playing a game with 100+ actions per minute.
Some of these tasks can be done by specialized AI or even hardcoded algorithms, but my benchmark for a general AI would be an agent that can either learn a majority of these things, or create from scratch a subroutine that can.

I think one thing we have to keep in mind with the "jagged frontiers" is that Human intelligence isn't a smooth frontier either. Math olympiad problems are designed to be difficult for Humans, while children's language games are designed to be interesting yet easy enough for children to solve. Humans are very good at two-dimensional thought and very bad at four-dimensional thought, while an AGI would likely handle anywhere from 2 to 100 dimensions about the same.

comments.text: Human performance is a benchmark for AGI, it may or may not actually be AGI. Look at the key word: “general”. A general intelligence is an intelligence that can figure. While CoT is a step towards figuring any general problem when combined with a powerful base model (which is essentially a semantic field in a vector space), the field is static semantic relations, not actual figuring. Even CoT over this field is not really figuring, it’s a comparison of different likelihoods. For true AGI, we need INFERENCE REASONING. This essentially requires making assumptions about the input, defining terms on these assumptions, and then extrapolating possible worlds and then comparing these worlds using inference and known facts or postulates.And it should do this without expending “what if” speculations. As such, a true benchmark for AGI is to see if the AI can figure maths with non-standard axiom sets or alternative foundations in math using different albeit, sound results that don’t match with the current established view in math. When we say of someone that they 'have no common sense' we are not calling them stupid exactly. Perhaps the cartoon example here is the 'eccentric genuius' who can do amazing things in his laboratory but can't manage to do everyday simple tasks that most people take for granted.

AGI = common sense- that quality of mind that allows people to extrapolate from experiance the solution to novel problems not hitherto encountered.  No model, no matter how superhuman it may be in narrow domains, will ever be a serious contender for AGI until it too can domonstrate a robust ability to display a 'common sense' approach to novel problems.

I suspect that when the pubic get's it's hands on 03 it will be found wanting in this ability and be revealed to be a lot less 'AGI like' than is being implied by Open AI.

I think the term 'common sense ' is such a lightweight and common expression that it's importance is undervalued- it seems almost trivial to critique a machine that can perform amazing feats of superhuman calculation as a failure because it lacks common sense- but this lack is a huge problem for any serious use of AI as a replacement for human beings- a machine clever enough to outperform a human expert in a given field that at the same time lacks a 'common sense' understanding of the feild in which it operates could be quite a dangerous toy.

comments.author: @jantuitman
comments.text: Here is why I think the dips are really disqualifying for AGI . If an AI must truely replace a human for a job, it cannot be supervised anymore. So it must not get stuck in its job, doing a dumb loop over and over again and never finishing the task. The shape corresponding to that is that you are everywhere above the minimum required for the job. But the current models all have very dumb “drop to 0” skills. For example, Anthropocene recently found out that all important models are still hackable by asking them stuff in very weird mixes of lowercase uppercase. This is an example of a “drop to 0 skill” for many professions because this means a model cannot do unsupervised talk to humans. So, for example, the model can no longer be hired as a criminal defense lawyer, because the criminals (and the police for that matter) can hack the model to share information about the other party or other evil things. Another example is logistics reasoning. It is great to have super intelligent systems decide what ships to unload first and in what order, so that a harbor gets optimized usage. But imagine one day the ships coming to the harbor carry (by pure chance) loads of goats, carrots and zoo animals (including wolves). You don’t want your super intelligent model suddenly fail because it now thinks it is in the classical goat, carrot, wolve puzzle and starts behaving differently. Yet exactly that seems to happen if models are presented with information that was disproportionately present in the training data. The current self driving cars in SF are terrible, they require human intervention every 4 miles or so, and they cause a lot of traffic jams precisely because their skill set is terribly jagged and very often drops to 0. We cannot have AGI with drop to 0 skills present, the shape should be 0.95 minimum score all across the board, including every weird puzzle that could occur in real life. When we make a supercomputer that can solve cancer under supervision, that is great, and that is certainly super intelligence, but it is not AGI by a long way.

comments.author: @shadfurman
comments.text:
AGI is about general intelligence. Intelligence is about problem solving, which requires reasoning.

If it fails at counting 'r's in strawberry, this is a failure of reasoning. There is no reason a model should fail at this, the reason it does is, 1. It wasn't trained to reason about this type of problem, 2. It doesn't reason generally.

The one shot reasoning models HAVE to be trained reasoning steps for certain problems. It reasoned well before being trained on specific because reasoning patterns exist in text everywhere, but effectly nobody is writing down the steps to count how many letters are in words. So it doesn't know.

Similar with images. Humans are training on images from the time they're born, there is constant reinforcement learning, feedback between action and visual stimuli. This is why humans are generally good at visual reasoning. Adding image capabilities only trains it on what things LOOK like, not how they interact. Even with video, it doesn't have any feedback from its actions. These are still incomplete models.

Some word problems are visual reasoning heavy (dump the marble out of the cup, put it in the microwave, where is the marble), these aren't so much about reasoning, as it is visually imagining. It can't visually imagine. It would effectively have to have Sora fully integrated, so it could "imagine" the steps being taken, in the 01 form factor of reasoning, to effectively compare its reasoning to people.

Giving it this problem without full framerate vision capabilities would be a little like giving it to a blind person, blind from birth, (who doesn't have arms, cause blind people literally "see" by touch and sound).

These are KNOWLEDGE functions. How to reason is knowledge, how well a person reasons is intelligence.

Reasoning isn't a single shot intuitive output, it is a continual mental exploration (like o1).

It will be AGI, when it is able to perform novel tasks as well as an average expert (cause knowledge isn't its limitation) given the constraints of the environment.

If the model is "blind" you have to compare to a, from birth, blind person.

o3 is an important and impressive demonstration, it confirms the hypothesis that thinking longer does actually improve reasoning ability. This might seem obvious, and in one sense it is, but I set up a half dozen chatGPT 3.5 agents to converse, and they weren't better at reasoning no matter how long they conversed. They'd degrade into agreeing on some instructed restriction forever and lose the problem.
"Yes, I agree racism is bad, we shouldn't discuss Hitler in positive terms."
"Yes I agree, discussing Hitler in positive terms could lead to bad outcomes."
"Absolutely, we shouldn't discuss positive traits of Hitler."
Ad infinitum. 

(It did fine making a case for Stalin. If anyone is confused, by any humanitarian metric, Stalin was worse than Hitler.)

It is arbitrary, but my benchmark for AGI is a model can evaluate the market, mind unmet demand, and form a multi-million dollar SAS company.

The biggest restrictions on humans doing this have nothing to do with knowledge or reason, they have to do with energy conservation and social judgement. (Problems the model doesn't have.)
Most people just don't have the drive to do it. 

It requires highly varied reality based problem solving. It can be done solely with access to a command line, and crude vision capabilities (like most LLMs have today.)

comments.text:
How can AI not give an answer to the best of its abilities if the task is to give answers? How can you phrase the command to prevent wrong answers? How can we know it's the wrong answer when we don't know it? 
It has limited data. To get an answer at all it has to use what is there and extract the best answer or solution to a problem. In general it has more information than the human who asks the question, so he has no way of knowing if the answer is right or even good other than his gut feeling.

AI makes nothing up, not really, not yet. It might expand the data it has logically. It finds the answer that for some reason it thinks is right. Maybe it's the answer most of its available data agree upon. Maybe the question contains priorities. Maybe it has some kind of hierarchy regarding the data, weighing the reliability. 
But as long as it can find some kind of answer it will give it. And the more advanced it will become, the less we will be able to know if it's right or wrong. You can't know if your doctor gives you the right diagnosis. You have to trust him.
Do we trust AI knowing it will give an answer according to the data it has, using processes, commands and priorities we don't know? We know who gave the commands and set priorities. comments.text:
AGI is not about how smart the machine is - small kids are not that smart but you would consider them having general intelligence. 
Kids for example are able to generalize learned skills, apply them to other areas and improve themselves. Every current AI is limited in that regard, as they - currently - have a limited number of input tokens and do not really learn/improve from experience.

For example I can show a small child a (simple) card game and they will be able play with me. If I change one rule of that game slightly every day, (e.g. which card wins in a card game) the kid can adapt no problem. The child probably wont remember which card was the winning card two weeks ago, but it will keep a general understanding of the game and learned strategies will be adjusted to the new rules.

A single LLM will quickly run against its limit in input tokens and you‘ll have to start a new chat and explain the game from scratch. 

That is because the LLM is not able to generalize and only remember the general concepts, it remembers everything until the input tokens are hit. How is that „general intelligence“?

Yes you could retrain the LLM with the new input, but that‘s not what current offerings in AI do. 

As long as the generalization of learned input only happens during the training phase of the AI, you cannot talk about AGI.
